source.title: Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity: Experimental Evidence in LLM-Assisted Consulting, Data Analyst, and Management Tasks

page_placements.theme: Scaling-related quality gains can extend to productivity and revenue

record.file_problem: The supplied text is complete. Its paper title is “Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity: Experimental Evidence in LLM-Assisted Translation,” which differs from the title supplied in the record request.
record.tranche_reason: It measures how LLM training compute relates to human productivity and translation quality in a new setting, rather than measuring language-model held-out loss or compute-optimal training allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports an experiment relating model compute to human task time, translation grades, and earnings per minute. These are economic outcomes of people using LLMs, not measurements of model pretraining loss or model-alone downstream performance, so the rows are recorded under none of the listed versions. The no-AI versus any-AI comparison is not a compute-scaling result and is not included as a row. Cited language-model scaling results are not this study’s results. The aggregate productivity forecasts are derived projections, not experimental measurements.
record.test_reason: The study regresses human translators' time, grades and earnings on the training compute of the LLM they were given. These are outcomes for people using models, not model loss or model-alone downstream performance. Under the gate rules, studying a behaviour's effects on people without measuring the models themselves is not a test. It cites Kaplan et al. and borrows the scaling-law framing for economic outcomes, so it discusses the claim but tests no version. The record's 'tests/T3' is therefore downgraded.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. It should add that the authors use these estimates, in an Acemoglu/Hulten framework, to project at least about 6.9% US productivity growth over a decade from continued model scaling. The authors frame this projection as a likely lower bound.
record.recipe_differences: A randomized experiment measuring human translation productivity and quality while participants used assigned LLMs; unlike the original scaling-law studies, it does not measure held-out language-model loss or fit model-training loss curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The time effect differs by baseline translator skill: 4.9% per 10x compute for the high-skill group and 21.1% for the low-skill group. The study covers Spanish, Hindi, and Arabic translation tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Each 10x in the assisting LLM's training compute is associated with 12.3% less task time, +0.25 grade points (0.18 SD), and +16.1% earnings per minute for professional translators. This holds across 13 models spanning about two orders of magnitude of compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human productivity on LLM-assisted tasks improves log-linearly with the assisting model's training compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Time savings per 10x compute are larger for lower-skilled translators: 21.1% versus 4.9%, with the difference at p=0.017.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains from larger LLMs in assisted work are larger for lower-skilled workers.

record.problems: The study tests only professional translation and short tasks, and the authors state that the results cover just over two orders of magnitude of compute. Its outcomes are human-assisted economic outcomes, not language-model held-out loss. The paper itself says generalization to other domains and larger compute levels requires further research. The reported time-scaling estimate is not fully consistent across the text: 12.3% in the abstract and Section 3.2 versus 12.65% in the Figure 2 caption.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results left out. The projected aggregate productivity estimates in Section 4 are derived from assumptions and experimental estimates, not separate experimental measurements.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured.
There is no fit on small runs or extrapolation of loss.
There is no parameter/token allocation at fixed compute.
No power-law loss is measured in other modalities or training regimes.
No model-alone downstream performance is measured; only human-assisted outcomes against compute are reported.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents is made.

record.verdict_notes: This is a preregistered RCT with 300 translators and 13 LLMs; individual models and their compute estimates are not listed. The compute axis runs roughly 10^23.5 to 10^26 FLOPs, and compute values are presumably external estimates. No model loss or model-alone benchmark appears anywhere, so none of V1–V7 is tested. The record's title mismatch note is accurate.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit small-run loss curves or test their predictions on larger runs.
It does not compare parameter and token allocations at fixed training compute.
It does not vary depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
It studies translation tasks with LLM assistance, but does not test power-law loss scaling across modalities or training regimes.
It measures human performance on translation tasks with LLM assistance, not performance of the language models themselves on downstream tasks or its relation to pretraining loss.
It does not compare loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices or training setups.

rows.measure: Task completion time versus log10 model training compute
rows.value: 12.3% reduction in time per 10x compute; Appendix A Table 3 reports a log-time coefficient of -0.0956 (standard error 0.0375) in one specification and -0.0933 (standard error 0.0363) in another

rows.note: The text also gives 12.65% in the Figure 2 caption, while the abstract and Section 3.2 report 12.3%. The result concerns participant time, not model loss.
rows.check: A baseline exists: the any-AI mean was 413.8 s versus 600.7 s without AI. In-text table references are off by one from the Appendix numbering; the time regression is Appendix Table 3. The 12.3% figure is at odds with the Figure 2 caption's 12.65%.

relation.reason: The paper discusses established loss scaling as motivation for studying economic outcomes, but does not measure model loss, compute-optimal allocation or model-alone downstream performance.

tranche.reason: The experiment measures human translation time, submission quality and earnings with LLM assistance. These outcomes do not directly test V1–V7 under the rules excluding effects on people without measurements of the model behavior itself.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv:2409.02391v2, titled Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity: Experimental Evidence in LLM-Assisted Translation; the pack's consulting/data-analysis/management title does not match. The paper itself has inconsistent time estimates: 12.3% in prose, 12.65% in Figure 2, and log-time coefficients −0.0956/−0.0933 in Table 3; prose appendix references are off by one.
